source.title: The formation and evolution of early-type galaxies : solid results and open questions

accepted.question_text: How did massive early-type galaxies form and evolve, given that early-type galaxies are elliptical and lenticular galaxies and that observations indicate massive systems formed at redshift z > 2 on very short timescales? A self-contained answer should identify which physical channels among starbursts, mergers, secular evolution, and smooth gas accretion can build massive spheroids at high redshift, and should explain how candidate precursor populations selected at z > 2 relate to the later early-type galaxy population.
accepted.context_brief: Formation channels for massive early-type galaxies

evidence.quote: HOW DID MASSIVE EARLY-TYPE GALAXIES FORM ?

The properties of ETGs illustrated in previous sections indicate that the massive systems formed at z > 2 with very short timescales. Examples of precursor candidates have been found amongst starburst galaxies selected at z > 2 with a variety of techniques: sBzK

The emerging scenario indicates that, in addition to merging, also secular evolution and smooth accretion of gas play a role in building up disks and massive spheroids at high redshifts, even without major mergers

accepted.question_text: How could a substantial population of old, massive, passively evolving early-type galaxies have assembled by redshift z approximately 2.5, when the Universe was still young and when galaxy formation models available in 2004 did not expect such systems? The question includes whether active galactic nucleus feedback, together with supernova feedback, can rapidly quench star formation during the high-redshift formation of massive early-type galaxies.
accepted.context_brief: Early assembly and quenching of massive passive galaxies

evidence.quote: The existence of a substantial population of old, massive, passively evolving ETGs up to z ≈ 2.5 was not expected in the galaxy formation models available in 2004
This raised the critical question on how it was possible to assemble such systems when the Universe was so young.

A promising mechanism is the AGN feedback which, in addition to that of SNe, would allow the rapid suppression ("quenching") of the star formation during the formation of massive ETGs at high redshifts

accepted.question_text: What explains the compact sizes of early-type galaxies at redshift z > 1, and how do these superdense galaxies increase their sizes enough to match the local Kormendy relation by redshift z approximately 0? The problem concerns early-type galaxies with effective radii Re ≤ 1 kpc, sizes about 2--3 times smaller than present-day early-type galaxies, stellar mass surface densities up to about 10 times local values, and stellar volume densities up to about 30 times local values; it also asks whether the apparent size differences could be affected by observational biases such as surface-brightness dimming and signal-to-noise effects.
accepted.context_brief: Size evolution of compact high-redshift early-type galaxies

evidence.quote: Another property which characterizes ETGs at z > 1 is their compact structure [28], with sizes (Re ≤ 1 kpc) much smaller than in present-day ETGs.

Several studies have confirmed this property and showed that Re is typically smaller by a factor of ≈ 2-3 than at z ≈ 0, implying that the stellar mass surface and volume internal densities are up to ≈ 10 and ≈ 30 times larger respectively

This is difficult to explain with simple passive luminosity evolution models and requires that these "superdense" ETGs should somehow increase their size in order to match the local Kormendy relation at z ≈ 0

It is unclear how to explain these size properties in the context of ETG evolution, and subtle observational biases (e.g. surface brightness dimming and S/N ratio effects) should not be completely excluded yet.

accepted.question_text: Are candidate early-type galaxies at redshift z > 3 genuinely old, passive, massive galaxies, or are most of them heavily dust-enshrouded starbursts whose spectral energy distributions mimic passive systems? The question arises because current studies at these redshifts rely on photometric redshifts and spectral energy distribution fitting rather than spectroscopy, and because a small subset of candidates at redshift z approximately 4--5 appears consistent with massive galaxies of mass about 10^11 solar masses, low dust extinction, and the oldest stellar ages allowed at those redshifts, pending confirmation by future facilities such as JWST and extremely large telescopes.
accepted.context_brief: Nature of z > 3 early-type galaxy candidates

evidence.quote: EARLY-TYPE GALAXIES AT z > 3 ?
However, at these redshifts, the current studies have to rely only on photometric redshifts and SED fitting analysis because spectroscopy is unfeasible.
Due to the degeneracies in the SED fitting analysis, most of the ETG candidates at z > 3 can be either heavily dust-enshrouded starbursts or old/passive galaxies

However, a small fraction does not show degeneracies and is formally consistent with being massive galaxies (M ≈ 10^11 M⊙) at z ≈ 4 − 5 with low dust extinction and the oldest ages allowed for these redshifts
If confirmed by future studies (e.g. JWST, ELTs), this population of massive, evolved galaxies would contribute significantly to the total stellar mass density at z ≈ 4 − 5

accepted.question_text: How can major dissipationless, or dry, merging explain the gradual size increase of compact, superdense early-type galaxies at 1 < z < 2 while remaining consistent with the observed small-scale clustering of low-redshift early-type galaxies and the weak evolution of the high-mass end of their stellar mass function at 0 < z < 0.7? The question asks whether dry merging is viable as the main size-growth mechanism or whether other processes such as smooth envelope accretion or multiple frequent minor mergers are needed.
accepted.context_brief: Viability of dry merging as a size-growth mechanism

evidence.quote: The compact, superdense ETGs at 1 < z < 2 evolve by increasing gradually their sizes. A possible mechanism is major dissipationless ("dry") merging

However, it is unclear how the "dry" merging scenario can be reconciled with the properties of the small-scale clustering of low-z ETGs [73, 74] and with the weak evolution of the high–mass end of their stellar mass function at 0 < z < 0.7.
Other processes which may increase the sizes at z < 1 are the smooth envelope accretion [79] and multiple frequent minor mergers [10].

accepted.question_text: What are the luminosity and stellar mass functions of early-type galaxies at redshift z > 1, and how can they be constrained robustly despite strong clustering and high cosmic variance? The problem focuses on obtaining wide-field survey measurements sufficient to determine the abundance of massive early-type galaxies at 1 < z < 3, where the strongest evolution and assembly of massive early-type galaxies is inferred to have occurred.
accepted.context_brief: Mass and luminosity functions at z > 1

evidence.quote: The results outlined in the previous sections indicate that the critical redshift range where the strongest evolution and assembly of massive ETGs took place is at 1 < z < 3
Preliminary estimates indicate that the number density of massive ETG photometric (pBzK) candidates at 1.4 < z < 2.5 is ≈ 20% of that at z = 0 [63].
However, due to the strong clustering and the consequent high cosmic variance, more wide-field surveys are needed to constrain stringently the luminosity and mass functions of ETGs at z > 1.
